title: M&S Launches 1,000-Strong Traineeship to Combat Youth Unemployment Crisis
summary: Facing a worsening youth unemployment crisis, British retailer Marks & Spencer is launching a major initiative: 1,000 paid traineeships for young people over the next 18 months. The program, aimed at 16-to-24-year-olds in the UK and Ireland, is a direct response to the alarming rise in so-called NEETs—those not in employment, education, or training. A recent government-commissioned review warned that without intervention, one in six young people could be NEET within five years, risking a “lost generation.” The M&S scheme offers six months of hands-on retail training, with successful participants eligible for further development toward store manager roles. Crucially, no degree is required. “We want more young people to see retail not just as a first job, but as a career with real opportunity, real responsibility and real progression,” said retail director Thinus Keeve. The move comes as entry-level positions across industries are shrinking, a trend exacerbated by the pandemic, smartphone distraction, and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence. The government has separately announced a partnership with industry and trade unions to examine how AI is reshaping entry-level roles, and pledged AI and tech training for 400,000 students in disadvantaged schools. For young people like Jess McGhee, who struggled to get callbacks before honing her skills at a youth employment hub, such programs can be life-changing. M&S’s investment signals a belief that retail can still offer a viable career ladder—if companies are willing to build it.
why_it_matters: For middle schoolers thinking about future jobs, this story reveals how technology and economic shifts are changing what 'entry-level' means. It shows that companies and governments are experimenting with new ways to give young people a fair start, raising questions about what kind of training and education will truly matter in an AI-driven world.

background_read: Marks & Spencer (often called M&S) is one of Britain's most famous retailers, with a history dating back over 130 years; it sells clothing, home goods, and high-quality food.

Youth unemployment has been a stubborn problem in the UK for over a decade, with the number of NEETs (young people not in employment, education, or training) rising after the 2008 financial crisis and again during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Economists worry that a 'lost generation' of young people who miss early work experience will struggle with lifetime earnings and skills, something seen in previous recessions.

A government-commissioned review recently warned that without intervention, one in six young people could be NEET within five years, prompting both policy responses and corporate initiatives like this one.

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence is now reshaping entry-level jobs, leading the government to partner with industry and trade unions to study this impact and to pledge AI training for 400,000 students in disadvantaged schools.

perspectives.description: Traineeships give young people hands-on experience and a clear path to manager roles without needing a university degree. This opens doors for those who might not afford higher education and proves that retail can be a meaningful, stable career.

One thousand positions over 18 months is a small number compared to the scale of the crisis; millions of young people remain at risk. Retail jobs also tend to be low-paid and insecure, so the programme may just be a temporary fix rather than a guaranteed ladder out of poverty.

This initiative reflects a broader economic reality: as automation and AI replace traditional entry-level tasks, companies must invest more in training their own workforce. It's a shift from hiring 'ready-made' workers to building skills from the ground up, which could remake the employer-employee relationship.

If successful, M&S's model could be copied by other large retailers and sectors, potentially changing how school-leavers find their first jobs. However, the government will need to ensure that AI training keeps pace with technological change, or else even these traineeships may become outdated within a few years.
